title: Molecular Speeds and Effusion
short: At one temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy, so lighter molecules move faster and effuse faster: rate ∝ 1/√M.
trouble: Students think heavier molecules have more kinetic energy at the same temperature, or forget the square root in Graham's law.

blocks.html: The Kinetic Molecular Theory pictures a gas as molecules in constant motion. How fast do they actually go? Faster than a passenger jet. And lighter molecules go faster still, which you can use, with Square Roots and Perfect Squares, to tell gases apart.

At a given temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy per mole, $\tfrac{3}{2}RT$. Because $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, lighter molecules must move faster: $$u_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{\mathcal{M}}}$$ ($R = 8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)}$, $\mathcal{M}$ in kg/mol, $u$ in m/s). Graham's law for effusion through a tiny hole: $$\frac{\text{rate}_1}{\text{rate}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\mathcal{M}_2}{\mathcal{M}_1}}.$$

Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so two gases at the same temperature share the same average $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. If one molecule is 16 times heavier, its $v^2$ must be 16 times smaller, so its speed is 4 times smaller: speed goes as $1/\sqrt{\mathcal{M}}$. Effusion is molecules escaping through a pinhole one by one, so the escape rate is proportional to how fast they arrive at the hole, which is proportional to their speed. That is Graham's law.

blocks.cap: Helium and argon at the same temperature, with a pinhole open. Argon atoms are 10 times heavier, so they move about $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$ times slower and escape more slowly.

blocks.title: How fast is nitrogen?
blocks.q: Find the root-mean-square speed of $\mathrm{N_2}$ molecules ($28.02\ \text{g/mol}$) at $25^\circ\text{C}$.
steps: Check the units: J/kg $=$ m²/s², whose square root is m/s.

blocks.title: Comparing effusion rates
blocks.q: How many times faster does $\mathrm{H_2}$ ($2.02\ \text{g/mol}$) effuse than $\mathrm{O_2}$ ($32.00\ \text{g/mol}$)?
steps: Graham's law with the lighter gas on top: $\dfrac{\text{rate}_{\mathrm{H_2}}}{\text{rate}_{\mathrm{O_2}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{O_2}}}{\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{H_2}}}}$.
$\sqrt{\dfrac{32.00}{2.02}} = \sqrt{15.84} = 3.98$: about 4, because oxygen molecules are about 16 times heavier.

blocks.title: Finding a molar mass
blocks.q: An unknown gas effuses $0.707$ times as fast as $\mathrm{O_2}$ under the same conditions. Find its molar mass.

blocks.html: Thinking heavier molecules have more kinetic energy at the same temperature, or leaving out the square root in Graham's law. All gases at one temperature share the same average kinetic energy; heavy ones simply move slower. A gas 16 times heavier effuses 4 times slower, not 16. Check: the lighter gas always effuses faster, by the square root of the mass ratio.
